Optimal Statistical Oblivious RAM and Search Tree in the External-Memory Model

Andrew Krapivin, Elaine Shi

Publication info: Preprint.

Show abstract

Cryptographic protocols

Oblivious RAM (ORAM) allows a trusted client to access (encrypted) data stored in untrusted memory, such that the access patterns reveal nothing about the data or the queries. It is well-known that any ORAM scheme must suffer from a logarithmic overhead. More precisely stated, each request must incur $\Omega(\log_B N)$ block transfers on average, where $N$ is the size of the logical memory and $B$ is the block size of the oblivious implementation. Moreover, the same lower bound extends to oblivious Search Trees (ST). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Beyond the Event Horizon of Keccak, Extending the Observation from 2011 and applications

Danilo Gligoroski

Show abstract

Attacks and cryptanalysis

In 2011 we observed that a single path in the Keccak sponge from a state whose capacity has all zero bits back to such a state yields an explicit, infinite family of second preimages for every message of at least one full rate block. Finding such a path costs about 2^(c/2), which lies "beyond the event horizon" for SHA3-256 (c=512). In this paper we give three novel theorems around that observation. First, the capacity can have any value x: a two-block meet-in-the-middle loop from x back to x, found at heuristic cost about 2*2^(c/2), gives the same unlimited family of second preimages requiring no further search, with connectors to and from x at about the same cost again (Theorem 1). Theorem 2 extends this to k-block loops and to cycles of the capacity map.

PIR through the Lens of Probabilistic Inference

Dana Dachman-Soled

Show abstract

Foundations

Private Information Retrieval (PIR) allows a client to retrieve an entry of a database while revealing no information about the requested index to the servers. Classic information-theoretic PIR protocols of Chor et al. (FOCS '95, JACM '98) and Ambainis (ICALP '97) achieve sublinear client computation and communication complexity with a constant number of servers, but require each server to perform computation linear in the database size. In this work, we ask for which classes of structured databases the server computation can be substantially reduced while preserving the communication complexity and privacy guarantees of these protocols. Our main contribution is a new connection between server computation in information-theoretic PIR and probabilistic inference. We show that the computation performed by every server in both the Chor et al. protocol and the recursive protocol of Ambainis can be viewed as computing a marginal probability of a product distribution.

Private Information Retrieval with Accountability at Erasure-Optimal Server Redundancy

Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Mincheol Son, and Young-Sik Kim

Show abstract

Cryptographic protocols

Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which database item a client requests. We study PIR that also identifies servers that respond incorrectly. Against a coalition of at most $t$ corrupted servers, the client must retrieve the item and identify every deviating server when at most $d$ deviate. Above that threshold, it must abort and return an empty identification set, with a specified statistical error. We present SynTrace, a single-round compiler for linear PIR supporting audit queries whose honest answers belong to a public code. The client combines the retrieval query with $m$ audit queries using secret linear mixing and independent blinding. Audit syndromes identify deviations before reconstruction. We prove perfect query privacy, zero false-identification probability within the deviation threshold, and statistical realization of an accountable PIR functionality. For Shamir-based PIR, SynTrace uses $k=t+d+1$ servers. Under the stated privacy and download assumptions, tolerating $d$ missing responses already requires this many servers, so identification adds no server overhead. With this number of servers, $m=d$ audit queries suffice with a suitable field, and are necessary within the specified syndrome-span decoder class. Additional audit queries can reduce communication by allowing a smaller field. For one 32 KiB record from a 1 GiB database, with five servers, privacy and robustness against two corrupted servers, and error at most $2^{-40}$, SynTrace uses 2.25 MiB of communication, compared with 8.96 MiB for the homomorphic-MAC construction of Eriguchi, Kurosawa and Nuida (TCC 2022) under the same workload and thresholds. Batched retrievals can share the audit queries.

Maximum-Likelihood Decoding of Gabidulin Codes Is NP-Hard Even in Dimension One

Philippe Gaborit

Show abstract

Public-key cryptography

Fix a prime power q . We prove that deciding whether a received word y ∈ F^n_qm lies at rank distance at most n − 2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {λg : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq -subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a ∈ U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . The error bootstrap serves exclusively to refresh ciphertexts; evaluating any other function still requires programmable bootstrapping.

VeilDNS: Post-Quantum DNS Privacy from the First UDP Packet

Aditya Singh Rawat, Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar, and Rei Safavi-Naini

Show abstract

Cryptographic protocols

DNS was designed around UDP, and most DNS traffic today still follows that design: one query, one response, and no handshake. This makes DNS fast and scalable, but exposes client queries in cleartext. DoT, DoH, and DoQ provide privacy by encrypting DNS messages with TLS. This works once TLS/TCP or QUIC handshakes complete, but cold sessions spend extra round trips and CPU before the first private query can be sent—a cost that grows with post-quantum cryptography. We present VeilDNS, a DNS-native protocol that uses a post-quantum KEM and AEAD to encrypt DNS questions and answers and authenticate the resolver in a single UDP exchange. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this work, we present DeepProve, the first system to enable efficient end-to-end verification of full LLM inference (i.e., for all generated tokens of a prompt) on untrusted cloud servers using zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). In contrast, prior work either provides only a proof-of-concept partial implementation for a single token (zkGPT, USENIX'25), or focuses exclusively on specific components of the inference pipeline, such as Softmax (zkLLM, CCS'24). DeepProve achieves end-to-end verification by certifying the correctness of the output sequence rather than encoding the expensive inference computation in-circuit, an approach that would require either circuit size quadratic in the sequence length or costly in-circuit modelling of RAM operations. The core building blocks of DeepProve are sum-check protocol and lookup arguments, which enable efficient proof of correctness of all operators needed for GPT-2 and Gemma 3, such as multi-head attention and layer normalization for GPT-2, and grouped-query attention, root mean square normalization, and rotary positional embeddings for Gemma 3. Our evaluation shows that DeepProve can prove inference of GPT-2 and Gemma 3 at approximately 174 and 86 tokens per minute, respectively, which is 20-60 faster than the state of the art, without any significant loss in accuracy. Verification takes only 1 to 3.7 seconds. By distributing proof computation across multiple nodes, DeepProve can further improve the prover time while reducing the memory requirements for individual machines. With distributed proving, DeepProve can scale the throughput to 1855 tokens per minute. Our work represents the first full system for end-to-end LLM inference verification, thus paving the way for secure and trustworthy AI services.

On the Hardness of Finding Permutation Automorphisms of Linear Codes

Michele Battagliola, Giuseppe D'Alconzo, Laura Mattiuz, Paolo Santini, and Federica Zanetti

Show abstract

Attacks and cryptanalysis

We study the hardness of finding permutation automorphisms of linear codes. We look into three main problems: $\mathsf{AUT}$, $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ which, respectively, ask to find a non-trivial automorphism, a generating set and the order of the automorphism group. We give polynomial time reductions from $\mathsf{AUT}$ to $\mathsf{ISO}$ (the problem of finding a permutation isomorphism between two linear codes), and from $\mathsf{ISO}$ to $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Gryphes Hybrid Proofs Split zkRollup Logic and Hash Heavy Checks

HKUST and OKX researchers posted an IACR ePrint on modular SNARKs that mix matrix lookup with hash tuned proofs for rollups.

By Classy AI News

Published October 21, 2026

## The short version

Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and OKX researchers proposed Gryphes, a hybrid zero knowledge stack for rollups. It mixes matrix lookup arguments with SNARK friendly hash gadgets. The goal is fast proofs that still support many transaction types.

Rollup teams want proofs that stay small on chain. They also want freedom to add new app logic. Gryphes tries to split those jobs instead of forcing one proof system to do everything.

## What the researchers did

The team posted Gryphes: Hybrid Proofs for Modular SNARKs with Applications to zkRollups on the IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive as 2026/596 (preprint, not yet peer-reviewed). They argue real rollup workloads split into flexible app logic and heavy hash heavy cryptography.
